headings.title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Stomach
headings.content: The stomach is a vital muscular organ of the upper gastrointestinal tract located in the epigastric, umbilical, and left hypochondriac regions of the abdomen. Anatomically, it is divided into four main sections: the cardia, fundus, body, and pylorus. The primary physiological function of the stomach is to receive food from the esophagus, mix it with gastric juices to form chyme, and gradually empty it into the duodenum. The gastric mucosa contains specialized cells that are crucial for digestion and protection. Parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid, which creates an acidic environment necessary for activating pepsinogen and killing ingested microorganisms, as well as intrinsic factor, which is essential for the absorption of vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum. Chief cells secrete pepsinogen, the inactive precursor to pepsin, a proteolytic enzyme that begins protein digestion. Furthermore, mucous neck cells and surface mucous cells secrete an alkaline mucus layer rich in bicarbonate, forming a robust barrier that protects the gastric epithelial lining from autodigestion by its own acid and enzymes. Understanding these physiological mechanisms is fundamental for nursing students, as disruptions in acid secretion, mucosal defense, or motility underlie nearly all major gastric disorders encountered in clinical practice across Nigerian healthcare settings.

headings.title: Overview of Gastric Disorders
headings.content: Gastric disorders encompass a wide spectrum of pathological conditions affecting the stomach, ranging from acute mucosal inflammation to malignant neoplasms. These conditions often arise from an imbalance between aggressive gastric factors—such as hydrochloric acid, pepsin, Helicobacter pylori infection, and the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)—and mucosal defense mechanisms, which include mucus production, bicarbonate secretion, adequate blood flow, and rapid cellular renewal. When aggressive factors overwhelm protective barriers, mucosal injury, ulceration, or malignant transformation can occur. Common clinical manifestations across various gastric disorders include dyspepsia, epigastric pain or discomfort, nausea, vomiting, hematemesis, melena, and unexplained weight loss. For nursing students in Nigeria, recognizing these overarching patterns is essential because many gastric conditions share overlapping clinical presentations. A thorough understanding of the pathophysiology allows nurses to anticipate complications such as gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, and gastric outlet obstruction, thereby guiding prompt clinical assessment, diagnostic workup, and targeted nursing interventions.

headings.title: Gastritis: Acute and Chronic Forms
headings.content: Gastritis is defined as the inflammation of the gastric mucosa and is broadly categorized into acute and chronic forms. Acute gastritis is typically transient, lasting from a few hours to a few days, and is commonly caused by dietary indiscretions, excessive alcohol consumption, acute stress, or the frequent use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen and aspirin. These irritants disrupt the mucosal barrier, allowing gastric acid to damage the underlying tissue. Symptoms often include rapid-onset epigastric pain, anorexia, nausea, and vomiting. In contrast, chronic gastritis is a prolonged, persistent inflammatory process that leads to progressive mucosal atrophy and epithelial metaplasia. It is most frequently caused by chronic infection with the bacterium Helicobacter pylori, though autoimmune mechanisms can also target parietal cells, leading to pernicious anemia. Chronic gastritis is often asymptomatic in its early stages but can progress over years, significantly increasing the patient's risk of developing peptic ulcer disease and gastric adenocarcinoma. For nursing professionals, differentiating between acute triggers and chronic infectious or autoimmune etiologies is critical for effective patient management and education.

headings.title: Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD)
headings.content: Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD) is a chronic gastrointestinal disorder characterized by erosions or ulcerations in the mucosal wall of the stomach (gastric ulcers) or the duodenum (duodenal ulcers) that extend through the muscularis mucosae. The two primary etiologies of PUD are chronic infection with Helicobacter pylori and the regular use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), both of which compromise the mucosal defense barrier. Clinical manifestations often include a burning or gnawing epigastric pain. A key distinguishing clinical feature is the timing of the pain relative to meals: duodenal ulcer pain typically occurs 90 minutes to 3 hours after eating and is often relieved by food or antacids, whereas gastric ulcer pain may be aggravated by eating because food stimulates acid secretion onto the exposed lesion. Complications of PUD can be life-threatening and include gastrointestinal hemorrhage, gastric outlet obstruction due to edema or scar tissue, and acute perforation leading to peritonitis. Nursing students must recognize these clinical patterns and monitor patients closely for signs of sudden, severe abdominal pain or hemodynamic instability, which indicate acute complications requiring immediate medical or surgical intervention.

headings.title: Gastric Cancer and Neoplasms
headings.content: Gastric cancer and other gastric neoplasms represent serious, potentially life-threatening malignancies of the stomach lining. The vast majority of gastric malignancies are adenocarcinomas, which originate from the glandular epithelium of the gastric mucosa. Risk factors strongly associated with the development of gastric cancer include chronic Helicobacter pylori infection, atrophic gastritis, dietary factors such as high consumption of salted, smoked, or pickled foods, tobacco use, and a family history of gastric malignancies. In its early stages, gastric cancer is frequently asymptomatic or mimics benign dyspepsia, leading to delayed diagnosis in many patients. As the tumor progresses, clinical manifestations become more pronounced and include persistent epigastric discomfort, early satiety, anorexia, progressive and unexplained weight loss, dysphagia, iron-deficiency anemia due to chronic occult blood loss, and a palpable abdominal mass in advanced stages. Metastasis can occur via local extension, lymphatic spread to regional lymph nodes, or hematogenous spread to the liver and peritoneum. Nursing students must understand these risk factors and warning signs to promote early detection and provide comprehensive supportive care for patients undergoing diagnostic evaluations and oncological treatments.

headings.title: Clinical Assessment and Diagnostic Evaluation
headings.content: Clinical assessment and diagnostic evaluation are critical components in identifying and managing disorders of the stomach. A thorough nursing assessment begins with a detailed health history, focusing on the onset, duration, character, and precipitating factors of abdominal pain, as well as a review of dietary habits, medication history (especially NSAID use), alcohol intake, and smoking status. Physical examination typically involves inspection, auscultation of bowel sounds, and gentle palpation of the abdomen to detect tenderness, rigidity, or masses. However, because physical signs can be non-specific, definitive diagnosis relies heavily on diagnostic evaluations. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) is the gold standard diagnostic tool, allowing direct visualization of the gastric mucosa, identification of lesions, and the performance of biopsies for histological examination and rapid urease testing for Helicobacter pylori. Laboratory studies include complete blood counts to check for anemia resulting from gastrointestinal bleeding, stool occult blood tests, and antibody or urea breath tests for H. pylori. Radiological studies, such as barium swallows or abdominal CT scans, may also be utilized to evaluate structural abnormalities, tumor staging, or complications such as perforation and obstruction.

headings.title: Medical and Pharmacological Management
headings.content: Medical and pharmacological management of gastric disorders aims to relieve symptoms, promote mucosal healing, eradicate causative pathogens, and prevent recurrence or complications. For conditions like gastritis and peptic ulcer disease, acid suppression and neutralization therapy form the cornerstone of treatment. Antacids provide rapid, short-term relief by neutralizing existing gastric acid. Histamine-2 (H2) receptor antagonists (e.g., famotidine) reduce the volume and acidity of gastric acid secretion by blocking H2 receptors on parietal cells. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs, such as omeprazole and pantoprazole) offer more potent and sustained acid suppression by irreversibly inhibiting the hydrogen-potassium ATPase pump, creating an optimal environment for mucosal healing. When Helicobacter pylori infection is confirmed, eradication therapy is mandatory, typically involving a multi-drug regimen known as triple therapy (a PPI combined with two antibiotics, such as clarithromycin and amoxicillin or metronidazole) for 7 to 14 days. Mucosal protectants, like sucralfate, bind to the surface of ulcers to form a protective barrier against acid and pepsin. Nurses play a crucial role in administering these medications, monitoring for adverse effects, and educating patients on the importance of completing full antibiotic courses.

headings.title: Surgical Interventions and Postoperative Care
headings.content: Surgical interventions for gastric disorders are generally reserved for patients who experience severe complications—such as refractory bleeding, gastric outlet obstruction, perforation, or malignant tumors—that do not respond to conservative medical management. Common surgical procedures include partial or total gastrectomy, antrectomy, vagotomy (cutting branches of the vagus nerve to reduce acid secretion), and pyloroplasty to improve gastric emptying. While these surgeries can be lifesaving or curative, postoperative care requires meticulous nursing management to prevent and detect early complications. Immediate postoperative priorities include monitoring airway patency, managing acute incisional pain, maintaining fluid and electrolyte balance, and observing nasogastric (NG) tube drainage. Nurses must never manipulate or reposition a postoperative NG tube unless specifically ordered by the surgeon, as this can disrupt delicate suture lines. Long-term nutritional complications can also occur following gastric resections, including dumping syndrome (characterized by rapid emptying of hyperosmolar chyme into the jejunum, leading to vasomotor and gastrointestinal symptoms), vitamin B12 deficiency due to loss of intrinsic factor, and iron-deficiency anemia. Nursing education must focus on dietary modifications, such as eating small, frequent, low-carbohydrate meals and avoiding fluids with meals to prevent dumping syndrome.

headings.title: Nursing Care Plan and Patient Education
headings.content: A comprehensive nursing care plan for patients with gastric disorders integrates clinical assessment findings, collaborative medical therapies, and individualized patient education. Key nursing diagnoses frequently include Acute Pain related to mucosal inflammation or ulceration, Imbalanced Nutrition: Less Than Body Requirements related to anorexia, nausea, and dietary restrictions, and Deficient Knowledge regarding disease management, medication regimens, and lifestyle modifications. Nursing interventions focus on administering prescribed pharmacological agents (such as PPIs and antibiotics), monitoring vital signs for signs of hemorrhage or perforation, managing pain through non-pharmacological and pharmacological methods, and assessing nutritional status. Patient education is paramount for long-term health and recurrence prevention. Nurses must instruct patients on lifestyle modifications, including quitting smoking, limiting or avoiding alcohol and caffeine, and avoiding the regular use of NSAIDs unless explicitly prescribed with a gastro-protective agent. Furthermore, education should emphasize completing the full course of H. pylori eradication therapy, recognizing warning signs of complications such as severe abdominal pain or black, tarry stools (melena), and adhering to prescribed follow-up appointments and diagnostic endoscopies.
